name: Starter: Swahili
about: Swahili noun classes and verbs in real, everyday sentences.

words.na: and, with; to have (nina: I have)
words.fanya: to do, to make (fanya kazi: to work)
words.kwenye: in, at, on; to (after going or coming)
words.kwa: for, by, to (kwa basi: by bus)
words.wahi: to be early; ever, before (sijawahi: I've never)
words.hivi: these (for a plural noun like viatu)
words.nyesha: to rain; to fall, of rain
words.julisha: to inform, to let someone know

habari-yako.about: The everyday greeting to one person, literally your news?; the answer is often Nzuri (good).

fanya-kazi.about: Literally to do work: anafanya kazi, she works.

piga-simu.en: to phone, to make a call
piga-simu.about: The person called goes inside the verb, which takes -ia: nitakupigia simu, I'll call you.

samahani.about: To get someone's attention or say sorry, to anyone.

naomba.about: A polite way to ask for something, literally I request: Naomba maji.

chakula-cha-jioni.about: Literally the food of the evening; lunch is chakula cha mchana.

hali-ya-hewa.about: Literally the state of the air.

items.means: One tea and some water, please.
I have a brother and a sister.
Excuse me, where is the bathroom?
Excuse me, how much is it?
My mother goes to the city.

items.text: Samahani, kituo cha treni kiko wapi?
items.means: Excuse me, where is the train station?
wrong: Samahani, kituo cha treni iko wapi?
Samahani, kituo cha treni uko wapi?

items.means: Tomorrow I'm going to the city.

items.text: Nina dada mmoja na kaka wawili.
items.means: I have one sister and two brothers.
wrong: Nina dada mmoja na kaka viwili.

items.text: Hili ni gari la baba yangu.
wrong: Hili ni gari cha baba yangu.

items.means: I don't know where they live.
My mom works at the hospital.
I live in a small house.
There's a book on the table.
There's no milk in the fridge.

items.text: Tuna jiko kubwa na roshani ndogo.
items.means: We have a big kitchen and a small balcony.
wrong: Tuna jiko kubwa na roshani mdogo.

items.text: Nikifika nyumbani, nitapika chakula cha jioni.
items.means: When I get home, I'll cook dinner.
wrong: Nikifika nyumbani, nilipika chakula cha jioni.

items.means: Could I have a glass of water?
I want to eat something sweet.
I like cooking with my mom.

items.text: Samahani, kituo cha basi kiko wapi?
items.means: Excuse me, where's the bus stop?
wrong: Samahani, kituo cha basi yuko wapi?

items.means: I'm going to the store to buy bread.
Tomorrow I'll go to work by bus.
The train was ten minutes late.
Grandma's waiting for us at the station.
On Saturday we're going to grandma's.
The ticket is a thousand shillings.
Are you coming to the movies with us?
We're going to the beach this weekend.
I've been learning Swahili since last year.
What are you doing this weekend?

items.text: Natumaini hali ya hewa itakuwa nzuri kesho.
items.means: I hope the weather's nice tomorrow.
wrong: Natumaini hali ya hewa itakuwa mzuri kesho.

items.means: If it rains, we'll stay home.

concept.line: A verb starts with who or what does it: ni- (I), u- (you), a- (he, she), tu- (we), m- (you all), wa- (they), and a thing's class (i- for treni), so mimi or wewe is often left out: ninasoma, unasoma, anasoma.
My (-angu) and your (-ako) come after the noun and take its class (jina lako: your name; viatu vyangu; funguo zangu: my keys), and many family words take y-: mama yangu, kaka yangu.
ni links someone or something to a name, kind, or description and never changes for am, is or are; its negative is si (Mimi ni mwalimu; Mimi si mwalimu), while location uses -ko forms instead.

words.means: nina = I have; una = you have; sina = I do not have
kiko = is; uko = is; iko = is; yuko = is

concept.line: Swahili has no words for a, an or the: Mimi ni mwalimu (I'm a teacher); Kuna kitabu mezani.

words.means: unazungumza = you speak; ninazungumza = I speak
sielewi = I do not understand; unaelewa = you understand

concept.line: -na- after the subject marker says it's happening now or usually (ninasoma: I read, I'm reading; anaishi: she lives), and with I, everyday forms often start with na- in place of nina-: napenda, nataka, naomba, natumaini.

words.means: ninaishi = I live; unaishi = you live; anaishi = lives
ninaenda = I go; unaenda = you are going; anaenda = goes

concept.line: Adjectives, this and that, and numbers usually follow their noun and show its class (viatu vipya; filamu hii; viatu viwili), while verbs show their subject's class (treni ilichelewa), but people take human agreement even when the noun looks different: dada mmoja, kaka wawili, kaka anasoma.

words.means: ninafanya = I do; kufanya = to do; nifanye = I should do
